title: It is finished (Luke 23:44–56)
hook: darkness, the veil torn, into thy hands, and a borrowed tomb

segments.voice: Yesterday, his mother stood at the foot of the cross, and he gave her to his friend. Your line was behold thy mother. Who did you look after? Day sixty-six. Today is the hardest hour of the story.

A Catholic church on Good Friday afternoon looks wrong on purpose. The tabernacle stands open and empty. The altar is stripped bare: no cloth, no candles, no flowers. There's no Mass. On this day and the next, the Church celebrates none. The priest walks in and lies face down on the floor, or kneels, in silence. Then the Passion is read aloud, the whole story, and at one moment everyone in the church kneels, and nobody says a word for a while. Today is that moment, the way Luke tells it.

It's about noon, and Luke says darkness covers the whole land until three in the afternoon. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was rent in the midst." The veil was the great curtain in the temple that hid the holiest place, where only the high priest went, once a year. Christians have read its tearing as the way to God being opened. Then Jesus cries out with a loud voice: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Those words aren't new. They're from a psalm, Psalm thirty in the Douay-Rheims, a prayer of trust, and he dies praying it. Today's title, it is finished, comes from John's Gospel, where the Douay-Rheims renders it "It is consummated." In Greek it's one word, tetelestai: it is finished, brought to its end. Two Gospels, two last words, and the Church keeps both. Then small, human things happen. A Roman centurion who has watched it all says: "Indeed this was a just man." The crowds go home beating their breasts. A council member named Joseph, from a town called Arimathea, who had not agreed with the others, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a tomb cut from rock where no one had ever been laid. The women from Galilee follow to see where. They go home, prepare spices, and rest on the Sabbath, as the law asked. And the Church's night prayer, at the end of every day, takes up his last words again: into your hands.
screen: `DARKNESS, AND THE VEIL TORN.` · `A PSALM ON HIS LIPS.` · `IT IS CONSUMMATED: BROUGHT TO ITS END.` · `A CENTURION, A TOMB, THE WOMEN.` · then, large: `FATHER, INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: silence. Settle and breathe. There's nothing to picture today and nothing to do. Just let it be quiet, the way the church goes quiet when everyone kneels. If thoughts come, let them go by. If you pray, you can say his words once, at the start, and then say nothing more: Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit. Then stay in the quiet until the bell. The bell holds the time.
It is finished. In John, one Greek word: brought to its end. In Luke, a psalm prayed with the last breath. Today's word.
Your line: into thy hands. Tonight, before you sleep, hand the day over, the good and the unfinished, in whatever words you have. Day sixty-six.

howItsDone: On Good Friday Catholics celebrate no Mass; they gather for the Passion, prayers, the veneration of the cross and communion from hosts consecrated the night before, and the Church's night prayer repeats the words into your hands.

original.note: Greek: it has been finished, brought to its end. one word in John 19:30.

trapdoor: what you thought: it is finished means it's over.
what it means: in John, the work is complete. in Luke, he dies praying a psalm, handing himself over: into thy hands.
what a scholar hears: tetelestai, a perfect-tense verb, done and staying done. and the torn veil hid the holy of holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 23:45–47 and John 19:30 given from memory; confirm.

Good Friday liturgy details (empty tabernacle, stripped altar, prostration of the priest, kneeling after the death in the Passion reading, no Mass) described from the Roman Missal in general terms; confirm.
The index hook says 'a borrowed tomb'; Luke says only a new tomb where no one had been laid (Matthew 27:60 says it was Joseph's own). The script does not use the word 'borrowed'.
Night prayer (Compline) responsory 'Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit' is in the modern Liturgy of the Hours; the English wording is copyrighted, so it is only mentioned, not quoted as such.
Title 'It is finished' is John 19:30 while the reading is Luke 23:44–56; the script explains both.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: 'the one day of the year the Church doesn't celebrate' Mass was wrong; the Roman Missal says the Church celebrates no sacraments (save penance and anointing) on Good Friday and Holy Saturday. Hook, screen and myth fixed. Also: hook no longer opens 'Walk into'; priest 'lies face down, or kneels' per the rubric; cut 'a prayer every faithful Jew would have known'; cut the 'debt paid in full' gloss on tetelestai (popular papyri claim, not in the cited text) from teach, word, match and original; 'Catholics say his last words every night' now attributed to the Church's night prayer; the veil detail is now sourced to Hebrews 9:3, 7.
